counterevidence: Capture-bearing turns are naturally high-leverage Mill decisions; observing captures in 16 of 19 first downgrades does not distinguish a removal-target error from a bad primary action or bad mill timing.
The cohorts are outcome-aware diagnostics, not random or preregistered inferential samples. Only 18 of 23 selected loss/control pairs also match prefix WDL.

Malom WDL has no repetition or fifty-move history and this audit does not use complete oracle step ordering. A WDL-preserving policy can therefore fail to convert a winning position before a live-rules draw.
One loss first drops from W to D. Because the audit stops at the first value downgrade, it does not locate that game's later D-to-L transition.
The audit never loads the candidate, so it cannot attribute a bad action to policy logits, temperature, sampling, or a particular feature route.
The result remains evidence from one training seed, one checkpoint, one fixed baseline and one frozen corpus.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Complete-turn choice around mill closure and compulsory removal is a plausible policy bottleneck.
hypotheses.support: Sixteen of 19 first value downgrades include a capture: all nine flying downgrades, three of four movement downgrades and four of six placement downgrades.
hypotheses.test: For each downgrade state, enumerate every complete legal turn with full corrected Malom ordering. Separate a wrong capture target under the same primary action from a wrong primary action or mill-timing decision.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The observed losses contain at least two failure regimes rather than one global collapse.
hypotheses.support: Six downgrades occur only two to five logical plies after the prefix during placement, while nine occur in flying with exactly three candidate pieces and a mean post-prefix ply of 46.11.
hypotheses.test: Keep placement and flying diagnostics separate, then freeze one intervention and measure it with phase-stratified fixed states and an unchanged held-out evaluator.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Some paired deficits are advantage-conversion and draw-history failures, not mistakes by the colour that eventually lost.
hypotheses.support: Four candidate losses begin already lost by WDL; in every corresponding colour-swapped game, the candidate has the favourable side but only draws.
hypotheses.test: Audit those four counterpart draws with full Malom move ordering plus repetition and no-progress history, locating the first loss of conversion progress even when coarse WDL remains winning.

next_validation: Run a read-only full-oracle alternative audit on the 19 first-downgrade states; do not ask the candidate to replay or sample any corpus move.
Audit the four favourable-colour counterpart draws with complete Malom ordering and live-rule repetition/no-progress counters.
Use those two audits to choose exactly one successor-training intervention and one matching ablation; do not bundle reward, curriculum and architecture changes.
Freeze train/validation diagnostics, multiple independent seeds, hyperparameters, data identities, baseline, ablation and per-class metrics before the successor retained run.
observed_facts: All 23 candidate losses and 23 deterministic non-reused matched draws were replayed from the immutable ledger with no Malom coverage gap.
Nineteen losses contain a candidate WDL downgrade; four are already losing for the candidate at the 12-ply prefix.
The 19 first downgrades are 18 draw-to-loss transitions and one win-to-draw transition.
First downgrades occur in six placement, four movement and nine flying states.
The six placement downgrades occur at post-prefix plies 2 through 5; the nine flying downgrades all occur with three candidate pieces.
Among the 18 loss/control pairs with equal prefix WDL, 17 losses have a downgrade and one starts lost; 16 controls have no observed downgrade, one has a win-to-draw downgrade and one starts lost.
Both colours lose from Perfect DB sources source-core-049 and source-core-058; these are the two full-point pair deficits.
